senses.gloss:
anvaṣṭakā
(‘after the अष्टक’)
------------------------------------------
Performing religious rites in honour of the departed ancestors and to satisfy their spirits is a universal phenomenon. In हिन्दुइस्म् such rites are called ‘śrāddha’ (literally, that which is performed with श्रद्धा or faith). The अन्वष्टका, also called anvaṣṭakya, is a śrāddha rite per-formed after the aṣṭakā rite (anu = after).
After establishing the fire and erecting a shed round it, offerings like boiled rice, pudding, preparations made out of curds as also liquor and scum of boiled rice are spread over बर्हिस् (sacrificial grass). After offering some portion into the fire, the rest are dedicated to the manes and their wives. The meat of an animal immolated on the aṣṭakā day should be cooked and offered to the ब्राह्मणस् invited for the ceremony.
The aṣṭakā type of śrāddhas gradually went out of vogue.
See also AṢṬAKĀ, PIṆḌAPITṚYAJÑA and ŚRĀDDHA.

anvādheya
(‘given after’)
------------------------------------------
Strīdhana or a woman’s property is an important topic discussed by the writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस्. A perusal of Vedic and early dharmaśāstra literature reveals that women had an honoured place in the Hindu society. References are not wanting to show that they were given gifts and endowed with property of which they could be independent owners (Ṛgveda 10.85.13 and 38; Āpastamba Dharmasūtras 2.6.14.9).
Among the five or six varieties of स्त्रीधन mentioned, अन्वाधेय is one. It is generally defined as what is obtained by a woman after (anu = after) her मर्रिअगे, from the family of her husband as also from the family of her ड़थेर्’s kinsmen. It could include all kinds of movable property.
See also STRĪDHANA.

anvitābhidhāna-vāda
(‘theory of related words’)
------------------------------------------
See ABHIHITĀNVAYA-VĀDA.

anvāhārya
(‘that which is made up’)
------------------------------------------
In the Darśa-pūrṇamāsa sacrifice the yajamāna (sacrificer) is advised to gift away cooked rice as sacrificial fee to the priests after cooking it on one of the fires, the दक्षिणाग्नि. This is meant to offset whatever defects might have been accrued to the sacrifice due to errors of omission and commission. This is called अन्वाहार्य.
Since अन्वाहार्य is cooked on the दक्षिणाग्नि, the latter is also called अन्वाहार्य-पचन.
A monthly śrāddha (religious rite in honour of the departed ancestors) performed immediately after पिण्डपितृयज्ञ is also called अन्वाहार्य.
See PIṆḌAPITṚYAJÑA also.

anvaya
(‘following or succession’)
------------------------------------------
The two words, अन्वय and व्यतिरेक, are frequently used in Indian works of philosophy and लोगिच् to prove a point. They invariably go together. अन्वय is a positive statement indicating a universal agreement whereas व्यतिरेक is the opposite of it, proving the same point by indicating the universal absence of the contrary.
To illustrate: Smoke is seen on the yonder hill. We conclude that there is fire on that hill. This conclusion is based on two premises from our previous experience:
Wherever there is smoke, there is fire;
Wherever there is no fire, there is no smoke.
Of these, the first one is a positive statement, asserting the presence of fire wherever there is smoke. Hence it is called अन्वय-vyāpti, or simply अन्वय. The second statement asserts a negative factor, the universal absence of smoke when there is no fire. This is called व्यतिरेक-vyāpti or व्यतिरेक (negation or contrariety). To prove the existence of fire on the hill on the evidence of smoke, both these methods of argument are necessary.

ānvīkṣikī
(‘science of reflecting after’)
------------------------------------------
Ancient works on polity often mention आन्वीक्षिकी as one of the four sciences to be taught compulsorily to the princes, especi-ally the one who will become the next king. Literally the word means something to be reflected upon (īkṣ = to reflect) after (anu = after) hearing about the same from the preceptor. Hence, the earliest connotation seems to be ‘philo-sophy,’ the same as was later on known as ‘darśana.’
However, the word has been used in later literature more exclusively to denote the logical sciences, tarkaśāstra or न्याय.
